17. On a perusal of the judgement of the trial Court, we find that the trial Court observed that there was no independent witness to support the claim of the plaintiff that Krishna Singha's mother handed possession of the suit land back to Irfan Ali Chowdhury. On the other hand, the trial Court highlighted the fact that the plaintiff's witnesses deposed that after Krishna Singha, his nephew Gopendra Singha was in possession of the suit land and that Gopendra Singha sold the suit land to defendant No.1. The trial Court observed that the evidence of P.W.3 Tara Miah supports the fact that the mother of Krishna Singha did not hand back possession of the suit land to Irfan Ali Chowdhury and that Krishna Singha did not abandon the suit land to go to India. It was observed that there was no documentary or oral evidence supporting the claim of Irfan Ali Chowdhury that he took physical possession of the suit land in 1342 BS. The trial Court further observed that the plaintiff did not lodge any diary or case with the police with regard to his dispossession from the suit land. It was noted that P.W.3 Tara Miah admitted in his cross-examination that Gopendra Singha went into possession of the suit land after Krishna Singha and, thereafter, sold the same to Makhon Miah (defendant No.1). It was also noted that P.W.4 in his cross-examination admitted that Monipuri people have been living in the suit property since 1950. 

 21. We note that the High Court Division mentioned that the trial Court after hearing the parties, without considering the evidence on record, wrongly and illegally dismissed the suit. However, we note from the impugned judgement that the High Court Division did not specifically refer to any of the evidence and materials on record to show which evidence the Courts below did not consider. The deed, by which Irfan Ali Chowdhury got the suit property is indeed very old. However, subsequent events and documents relating to those later events tend to indicate that Irfan Ali Chowdhury was no longer in possession of the suit land. On the contrary the evidence of the witnesses shows that defendant No.2 and his predecessors-in-interest were all along in possession of the suit land. We note that Krishna Singha, the predecessor of defendant No.1 got his name recorded in the record of rights as tenant, which the original plaintiff got corrected. But thereafter, Gopendra Singha (defendant No. 2 who sold the suit property to defendant No.1) filed an appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and got his name recorded in the record of rights. Khodeja Akhter Chowdhury who is the daughter of Irfan Ali Chowdhury deposing as P.W 1 could not controvert such claim. She admitted that her father's challenge against the record of rights was not fruitful. She also could not say whether her father took the matter further on appeal under section 53 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We note that P.W 1 stated in her evidence that her father took possession of the suit land in 1342 BS (c.1935 AD), whereas PW4 stated that in 1950 Manipuri people lived on the suit land. Coincidentally, in Title Suit No.301 of 1965, Irfan Ali Chowdhury had claimed that possession of the suit land had been handed over to him in 1362 BS. (c.1955 AD). Moreover, we note that P.W1 stated in her deposition that 1362 BS was mistakenly written and that the correct date was 1342. This is clearly falsified by the evidence of P.W4. 

 23. In view of the evidence of P.Ws 3 and 4 it is clear that the predecessors of defendant No.1 were in possession of the suit land in 1950, even according to the plaintiffs' own witness. Thus, about 15 years before defendant No.1 purchased the suit land, Monipuri people were in possession and there was no evidence that possession reverted to the original plaintiff at any time after 1950.
